blocks.prompt: 15 If \(a, b, c\) are in G.P., show that \(\log_a x, \log_b x, \log_c x\) are in H.P.
blocks.explanation:
A proof with logarithms. To show H.P., show the reciprocals are in A.P.
The reciprocal of \(\log_a x\) is \(\log_x a\).
Plan: show \(\log_x a, \log_x b, \log_x c\) are in A.P. using \(b^{2} = ac\).
steps:
Given: \(a, b, c\) are in G.P. (positive, \(\ne 1\)); \(x > 0\), \(x \ne 1\).
To prove: \(\log_a x, \log_b x, \log_c x\) are in H.P.
Method: \(\log_a x = \frac{1}{\log_x a}\) (change of base), so it is enough to prove \(\log_x a, \log_x b, \log_x c\) are in A.P.

G.P. condition
\[b^{2} = ac\]
Why: \(b\) is the G.M. of \(a\) and \(c\), i.e. \(\frac{b}{a} = \frac{c}{b}\).

Take \(\log_x\) of both sides
\[\log_x b^{2} = \log_x (ac)\]
\[2\log_x b = \log_x a + \log_x c\]
Why: Laws of logarithms: \(\log_x b^{2} = 2\log_x b\) and \(\log_x (ac) = \log_x a + \log_x c\).

Read it as an A.P.
\[\log_x a, \; \log_x b, \; \log_x c \text{ are in A.P.}\]
Why: Twice the middle term equals the sum of the outer terms.

Take reciprocals
\[\dfrac{1}{\log_x a} = \log_a x\]
\[\log_a x, \; \log_b x, \; \log_c x \text{ are in H.P.}\]
Why: Reciprocals of an A.P. form an H.P., and \(\frac{1}{\log_x a} = \log_a x\).

Check with numbers: \(a = 2, b = 4, c = 8\) (G.P.), \(x = 64\). Then \(\log_2 64 = 6\), \(\log_4 64 = 3\), \(\log_8 64 = 2\); reciprocals \(\frac{1}{6}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}\) have difference \(\frac{1}{6}\) each, so 6, 3, 2 is an H.P. \(\checkmark\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\log_a x, \log_b x, \log_c x\) are in H.P.
